messages.subject: Some questions on GMM for 3D data
messages.subject_clean: Some questions on GMM for 3D data
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone, I have some experience with GMM for 2D data but I am recently moving forward to 3D data. With such move, I come across some new problems.

1. I am using 3dMD to obtain 3D facial stereo-photogrammetric images of my participants. I noted that the margin of the images are irregular (see image blow)
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-yD5Em5ZxNg4/WjfNAUobi_I/AAAAAAAABpA/bnULRK92HbU5Y5d_OuWQnhbl3N02dq42QCLcBGAs/s1600/%25E6%2590%259C%25E7%258B%2597%25E6%2588%25AA%25E5%259B%25BE17%25E5%25B9%25B412%25E6%259C%258818%25E6%2597%25A52207_1.png>
It can be clearly seem from the image above that the margins of the imaged objects are serrated (indicated by the yellow arrow). More importantly, when I am studying facial shape using GMM, I am not interested in regions such as the neck in the above image. Although regions like the neck are unwanted, semilandmarks will still be automatically placed upon such regions when the samples are digitized in geomorph. I wish to know is there a way to trim off the unwanted regions from 3D data in ply format. Or should I use some other 3D digitization software that allows me to choose where to place semilandmarks?

2. How can I determine the optimal number of curve and surface semilandmarks to place on the region of interest?
Page 3 of the paper "Toward integration of geometric morphometrics and computational biomechanics" stated that "To determine the optimal number of landmarks for performing the warps,a separate sensitivity analysis was conducted using 5 different landmark configurations and densities ranging from using 92 single landmark points to using a combination of 20 single landmarks in addition to 540 pseudolandmarks and slid semilandmarks. Accuracy of warps was judged by warping the V. gouldii mesh to the target shape of the L. borneesis mesh and comparing the bending displacement in the warp with that in the original L. borneesis." However, I still do not know how the "warps" and the "bending displacement" were determined. Can geomorph or any other software help in such determination?

3. After statistical analyses, say regression of shape on centroid size, I obtained procrustes coordinates of the predicted facial shape of the specimens at a particular centroid size. Now I wish to visualize the predicted facial shape, not by separate landmarks as can be obtained from the plotAllSpecimens function in geomorph, but with textures included. I want to know how can I obtain a 3D image of the predicted facial shape with textures included? What software should I use? Amira, Harpoon, Edgewarp (Linux system only?), Viewbox4, IDAV Landmark, or Stratovan Checkpoint?
.

messages.subject: Phylogenetically-corrected shape data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

For my current work, I'm attempting to implement a similar method to the phylogenetically-transformed measure of morphological disparity used a recent paper by Serb et al. (2017). Following the Adams (2014) method, I believe I have correctly phylogenetically-transformed my shape data, but I'm hoping someone would be willing to confirm this for me. Is my understanding correct in that multiplication of the shape data by the phylogenetic transformation matrix (E) results in "phylogenetically-corrected" shape data to which one could apply standard metrics of disparity? (code below if needed). I don't want to do a regression, which is why I haven't used the geomorph morphol.disparity() function and have opted for this method instead.

My apologies for bothering you all with a relatively straight forward question, but it would ease my mind knowing I didn't make some grave calculation error. My phylogenetically transformed shape data are behaving somewhat strangely in my downstream analysis and wanted to make sure this wasn't the culprit.

Much appreciated,
Sarah

Code for clarification:
y <- shapedata
x <- sizedata
C <- vcv.phylo(tree)
eigC <- eigen(C)
U <- eigC$vectors
W <- eigC$values
E <- solve(U %*% diag(sqrt(W)) %*% t(U))
y_cor <- E %*% y
x_cor <- E %*% x

messages.body_plain:
Sarah,

Your math is correct, but I do not understand your comment concerning the phylogenetic options in morphol.disparity. It is not restricted to regression, but can accommodate single-group (ie total disparity), disparity comparisons for groups in a factor, or while accounting for continuous covariates.

At their heart, all variance-based disparity measures attempt to quantify residual variance from a model. Biologists typically do not think about it that way but they should.  For total disparity the model is: Y~1.  For disparity relative to groups, it is Y~group.  For the group comparison of disparity while accounting for phylogeny the command would be something like:

morphol.disparity(mypgls.res, groups= ~groups, data = gdf, iter=499)

Where mypgls.res represents a results object from procD.pgls (of groups), and groups are as specified as before.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
A few quick points.

1: look at the SS and MS for the shape effects. They are identical in both up to rounding error. Thus, any differences are downstream of the algebra and rest in how significance is assessed.

2: In that regard, MorphoJ uses parametric significance testing based on MANOVA. These are laden with many untenable assumptions for shape data: multivariate normality, homoscedasticity, assumptions linking multivariate to univariate test measures, etc.  By contrast, geomorph uses permutation tests to evaluate significance.

3: You are only using 19 permutations for significance testing in geomorph: that makes no sense. Bump that up to 999 or 9999 for more precise p-values.

This is where the issue starts: when I use gpagen and plotAllspecimens I don't get a proper result, with some individuals being completely distorted (see whitefish_no_missing_procrustes.png). I can't figure out the issue, I tried the unbend function in tpsutil but it doesn't seem to work. Also, when I load the whitefish_no_missing.TPS in MorphoJ this issue doesnt appear at all.

Has any of you encountered something similar before? I appreciate the help so close to the holidays.

Best wishes,

Marco

Dear Marco,

This is appears to be both an issue with readland.tps and your data, or at least, how they are working together.  readland.tps expects that you have 456 specimens but somehow is only recognizing 455 instances of points = 7 in your second curves.  At some point, the 7 curve points are read from the data from the next specimen, and then the problem cascades from specimen to specimen.

We will try to dig some more and see if this is purely a programming error, a quality control error (the function not catching some missing data), or something else, but unfortunately, your email catches all of us on holiday, so it might take a while to sort this out.  One thing you could do in the interim - if you want a quick solution - is remove all lines for curves and points from your tps file, and change LM=25 to LM=47 (the total of fixed landmarks and sliders) and try again.  For geomorph, the curves and points codes do not mean anything and the readland.tps function just turns these points into regular landmarks; curves are defined separately.

Sorry for the delay, but happy holidays!

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anderson,

I have some good news and some better news.  First, the reason for this error.  Your image names have the word “scale” embedded within then.  That throws off the readland.tps function when it searches for the scale.  It is a programming glitch because we did not anticipate “scale” in other locations than the scale line.  I have added code to catch something like this and the update is now available on Github.  As a reminder, how to update geomorph from Github:

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”)

That was the good news.  You can immediately update geomorph and you should have no issue now.  If your problem persists though, let us know.

We are also currently getting geomorph ready for an update to CRAN, which we expect to happen maybe in a few weeks (after we have some time to test our updates).  As it turns out, readland.tps is one of the functions we are updating.  The better news is that your TPS file did not trigger any issues with our new update.

Thank you for the indirectly provided opportunity to test our updated function!

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: How to know which semilandmark is symmetric relative to which semilandmark when I have thousands of semilandmarks?

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am doing 3D GMM on specimens with object symmetry. I have 28 landmarks, 7 curves, and 9 patches. The total number of curve and surface semilandmarks is 6522. When using bilat.symmetry function, I defined which landmark is symmetric with which landmark. I did this only for landmarks but not for semilandmarks. I then tried to obtain the 3D surface mesh of the mean shape of my specimens, which looks like below:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-PLQvPzhx87M/WkcpHQ5scCI/AAAAAAAABpg/sZKC7emVFnQtNNL3aRymCi_1XHt3sQcXwCLcBGAs/s1600/%25E6%2590%259C%25E7%258B%2597%25E6%2588%25AA%25E5%259B%25BE17%25E5%25B9%25B412%25E6%259C%258830%25E6%2597%25A51350_1.png>

It can be seen that those semilandmarks that should have been positioned around the midline are all compressed to the midline. It seems to mean that pairing relationship of semilandmarks also need to be specified in the land.pairs argument of the bilat.symmetry function. But I am really wondering how could I obtained the exact pairing relationships of the landmarks quickly and accurately in my case where there are thousands of semilandmarks.

Note that I placed smilandmarks in Checkpoint software and the digitization scheme looks like the folloing:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-FOMHWKYV_P0/WkcrdZIXsyI/AAAAAAAABps/tMPDxVWErlERVABw0fdyEZ48WwVE6YzhgCLcBGAs/s1600/%25E6%2590%259C%25E7%258B%2597%25E6%2588%25AA%25E5%259B%25BE17%25E5%25B9%25B412%25E6%259C%258830%25E6%2597%25A51359_2.png>

The blue dots represent the first semilandmark of each surface patch and the arrows indicate the ordering of semilandmarks. These are useful information when I wish to correlate each semilandmark with its mirrored one. But I am still confused as to how to quickly and accurately obtain such pairing relationship for thousands of semilandmarks.

Best regards,

Patrick
